decisions.reason: The authors preregistered five replication tests of Bellet et al. (2018). They report that the three statistically significant effects from Bellet et al. (2018)—on perceived posttraumatic vulnerability to self (PPVS-S), perceived vulnerability of others (PPVS-O), and the interaction between trigger warnings and belief that words can harm (WCHS) on immediate anxiety—did not replicate. Conversely, for the two effects that were nonsignificant (null) in Bellet et al. (2018), the replication found substantial evidence favoring the null hypothesis for anxiety sensitization (and in the full-sample open-alternative test for immediate anxiety, consistent with the original conclusion that trigger warnings do not reduce anxiety) and ambiguous replication-BF evidence for immediate anxiety. Because the replication confirms the original null findings on anxiety reduction/sensitization while failing to replicate the original significant vulnerability and WCHS moderation effects, the original-specific outcome is 'mixed'.

decisions.quote:
Method: Our experiment was a preregistered replication and extension of a previous one (Bellet, 

Jones, & McNally, 2018); 451 trauma survivors were randomly assigned to either receive or not 

receive trigger warnings prior to reading potentially distressing passages from world literature.
decisions.reason: The study collected new experimental data from a sample of 451 trauma survivors on Amazon Mechanical Turk to re-test the published experimental findings of Bellet, Jones, and McNally (2018), making it a replication.
